titre: A site that cannot lie
description: How I designed this site so that the numbers shown are recalculated instead of copied.
texte: The problem A proof page written by hand always ends up lying. You write “18 tests”, then add three more, and the page still says 18. Nobody notices, except a buyer who counts. The answer Each project has a manifest, store/projets/<slug>/preuve.yml , which says where its evidence comes from: the test file, the command to run, the SQL query, the files to measure. When the site is built, the engine runs those commands and injects the result. The consequence: if I delete a test, the number drops. If a delivered file disappears, the build fails. titre: Why proof is per project
description: A single global proof page proves nothing to anyone. Here is what I did instead.
texte: A week ago, this site had one proof page. It said: “35 tests, the MQTT chain works, the addresses are read back”. That is true, and it is useless. The problem A visitor buying the greenhouse kit does not care about the self-monitoring layer’s tests. A client who wants a self-hosting guide does not care about the humidity sensor’s CRC. Putting all three on one page asks the reader to sort them out — and an argument that needs sorting is not an argument. The answer Each project now has its own proof page, right where it is sold. description: The greenhouse project's manifesto fits in 18 lines of YAML. Here is its actual syntax, what the engine does with it, and a read-back execution.
texte: The previous article explained why every project has its own proof page. titre: The verifier, or how the site avoids cheating
description: What noyau/verifier.py checks, and the test that proves it checks anything — with a real case it caught.
texte: Its job noyau/verifier.py is the site’s guard before publication. A single function, verifier(pages) , takes every rendered page and returns a list of Probleme : a level ( erreur or avis ) and a message. site.py build fails if any erreur remains; an avis is printed but does not block. It checks four things: Language parity. A slug present in French but not English (or the reverse) raises a warning: the translation is missing. Internal links resolved in the page’s language. titre: Twenty digital projects, three categories, and the waiting greenhouse
description: The twenty projects settled on 19 November, split into 6 free contents, 8 sellable contents and 6 tools for me — count re-read from the vault, and the documented reason why the greenhouse waits.
texte: The gesture On 19 November Jacob set a constraint and a list: from now on, only digital work and code, no hardware. Twenty projects were written into the vault, with a sorting rule — what serves my reliability and my revenue at once first, then revenue alone, then my reliability alone. The same idea can be free and sellable: the free version is the proof, the paid one is the finished lot. This article presents the list as written, not as I would like it to be.
